'''''Liatris pycnostachya''''', the '''prairie blazing star''',<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |title=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=LIPY |website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref> '''cattail gayfeather''',<ref name="BONAP"/> '''Kansas gayfeather''',<ref name="Dyck Arboretum">{{cite web |title=The Gayfeathers |url=https://dyckarboretum.org/plant-profile-gayfeathers/#:~:text=Arboretum%E2%80%99s%20living%20collections.-,Kansas%20gayfeather,-or%20thickspike%20gayfeather |website=dyckarboretum.org}}</ref> or '''cattail blazing star''',<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1| tribe=Eupatorieae |first=Guy L. |last=Nesom}}</ref> is a [[perennial plant]] in the [[Asteraceae]] family that is native to the [[tallgrass prairie]]s of the central [[United States]].<ref name="BONAP">{{BONAP|ref |genus=Liatris |species=pycnostachya}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Pink |first=A. |date=2004 |title=Gardening for the Million |url=https://archive.org/details/gardeningforthem11892gut |publisher=Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation}}</ref>

==Description==
The flower stalks reach {{cvt|60|to|120|cm|ft|0}} in height, or rarely to {{cvt|180|cm|ft|0}}. The leaves are linear, grass-like, {{cvt|11|to|22|cm|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|4|to|10|mm|2}} wide.<ref name="FNA" /> They grow both from the root and in great numbers on the flower stems, becoming progressively smaller higher up the stem. The end of the flower stem is covered in a spike of [[flower head]]s {{cvt|1/4|to|1/2|in|mm|0}} across that bloom pink to purplish pink for a month in late summer,<ref>{{Illinois Wildflowers|prairie/plantx/pr_blazingstarx|Prairie Blazingstar (Liatris pycnostachya) |access-date=July 17, 2018}}</ref> from the top down.<ref name="Minnesota">{{Minnesota Wildflowers|flower/prairie-blazing-star|Liatris pycnostachya (Prairie Blazing Star) |access-date=July 17, 2018}}</ref> Each flower head has 5 to 8 [[floret]]s<ref name="FNA" /> and is surrounded by overlapping pinkish [[bract]]s ([[phyllaries]]) whose tips are pointed and curve backwards.<ref name="Minnesota" /> The stems, leaves, and bracts may be smooth or hairy to varying degrees.<ref name="FNA" /><ref>{{NPIN}}</ref> The shape of the bracts distinguishes this species from others, for example ''[[Liatris spicata]]'', another tall ''Liatris'' species that has thickly packed spikes, but whose bracts are flat with rounded tips.<ref>{{Illinois Wildflowers|wetland/plants/msh_blazingstar|Marsh Blazingstar (Liatris spicata) |access-date=July 17, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{eFloras|1|242413546|Liatris spicata |tribe=Eupatorieae |first=Guy L. |last=Nesom}}</ref>

The root system is a [[corm]] that sometimes develops into a [[rhizome]].<ref name="FNA" /> It produces offsets and gradually forms a clump.  

==Etymology==
The species epithet comes from [[Ancient Greek]] {{lang|grc|πυκνός}} ({{grc-tr|πυκνός}}) "dense" and {{lang|grc|στάχυς}} ({{grc-tr|στάχυς}}) "ear of grain",<ref>{{LSJ|pukno/s|πυκνός}} and {{LSJ|sta/xus|στάχυς|ref}}</ref> referring to the thickly packed spike of flowers.

==Distribution and habitat==
Its native habitats include prairies, open woods, and meadows.

==Ecology==
The plant attracts birds, hummingbirds, and butterflies.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Liatris pycnostachya - Plant Finder|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=d770|access-date=2022-01-18|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref>  It is a larval host to the [[bleeding flower moth]] (''Schinia sanguinea'').<ref>The Xerces Society (2016), ''Gardening for Butterflies: How You Can Attract and Protect Beautiful, Beneficial Insects'', Timber Press.</ref>
